title: Inputs that go to zero
objectives: Find the nullspace from the free variables.
Tell pivot variables from free variables after elimination.

screens.title: Back to the start
screens.prose: The matrix from last time has columns $\mathbf{a}_1 = (1, 2)$ and $\mathbf{a}_2 = (2, 4)$. The sliders set $x_1$ and $x_2$. This time we want $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ to end exactly at the origin.
screens.question: Which input $\mathbf{x}$, not both entries zero, sends $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ to the origin?

options.why: That works for every matrix, so it tells us nothing. Look for an input with a non-zero weight.
That gives $(1 - 2, 2 - 4) = (-1, -2)$. One copy of $\mathbf{a}_2$ is two copies of $\mathbf{a}_1$.
You put the 2 on $\mathbf{a}_2$. That gives $(-1 + 4, -2 + 8) = (3, 6)$.

hints.text: $\mathbf{a}_2$ is twice $\mathbf{a}_1$. How many copies of $\mathbf{a}_1$ does one $\mathbf{a}_2$ cancel?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try each pair on the sliders and watch where $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ ends.

explain.text: $2\mathbf{a}_1$ goes out to $(2, 4)$, and $-\mathbf{a}_2$ comes straight back. The chain ends at the origin, so $\mathbf{A}(2, -1) = \mathbf{0}$. A non-zero input can vanish.

screens.title: All the inputs that vanish
screens.prose: Now we look at the inputs instead. Each point is an input $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2)$, for the same $\mathbf{A}$. Drag $\mathbf{x}$ and read $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ below the grid.
screens.question: Where do all the inputs with $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ lie?

options.text: On the line through the origin and $(2, -1)$

options.why: Try $(4, -2)$: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = (4 - 4, 8 - 8) = (0, 0)$. Every multiple of $(2, -1)$ works.

options.text: On a line that misses the origin
options.why: $\mathbf{x} = (0, 0)$ always gives $\mathbf{0}$, so the origin is on it.

options.text: Everywhere: $\mathbf{A}$ flattens every input to zero
options.why: Try $(1, 0)$: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = (1, 2)$, not zero.

hints.text: Drag $\mathbf{x}$ to $(4, -2)$, then to $(-2, 1)$. Read $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ each time.

feedback.correct: Every multiple of $(2, -1)$ goes to zero, and nothing else does.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag $\mathbf{x}$ to several points where $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = (0, 0)$ and see what they share.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = (x_1 + 2x_2)(1, 2)$, which is zero exactly when $x_1 + 2x_2 = 0$. Those inputs form the line $x_2 = -\tfrac{1}{2}x_1$, through the origin and $(2, -1)$.

screens.title: The nullspace
screens.prose: The inputs with $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ form the **nullspace** $N(\mathbf{A})$. In 3D we find it by elimination. Take $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\end{pmatrix}$. One step clears row 2.

enter.caption: Row 2 is all zeros. One pivot, in column 1.

screens.question: Which unknowns can you choose freely, with the rest fixed by row 1?

options.why: $x_1$ sits in the pivot column. Row 1 fixes it once $x_2$ and $x_3$ are chosen.
Row 2 vanished, so it pins nothing down. Columns 2 and 3 both lack a pivot.
One equation cannot fix three unknowns. Only $x_1$ is tied down.

hints.text: After elimination, only row 1 says anything.
The pivot is circled in column 1. Columns 2 and 3 have none.
Row 1 reads $x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 0$. Pick $x_2$ and $x_3$, and $x_1$ follows.

feedback.correct: Columns 2 and 3 have no pivot, so $x_2$ and $x_3$ are free.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the columns that hold a pivot after elimination.

explain.text: Column 1 holds the pivot, so $x_1$ is a **pivot variable**. Columns 2 and 3 have none, so $x_2$ and $x_3$ are **free variables**. Row 1 then fixes $x_1 = -2x_2 - 3x_3$.

screens.prose: Set one free variable to 1 and the other to 0. Row 1 then fixes $x_1$. Each result is a **special solution**.
screens.question: Fill in $x_1$ for each special solution.

hints.text: Row 1 is the only equation left.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each row of the table must make $x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3$ equal to 0.

explain.text: With $x_2 = 1$, $x_3 = 0$, row 1 gives $x_1 = -2$. With $x_2 = 0$, $x_3 = 1$, it gives $x_1 = -3$. So $\mathbf{s}_1 = (-2, 1, 0)$ and $\mathbf{s}_2 = (-3, 0, 1)$, one per free variable.

screens.prose: Every combination $c_1\mathbf{s}_1 + c_2\mathbf{s}_2$ also satisfies row 1. So $N(\mathbf{A})$ is the plane through the origin spanned by $\mathbf{s}_1$ and $\mathbf{s}_2$.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which vectors are in $N(\mathbf{A})$?

options.why: $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$, not 0. Equal entries do not make the row vanish.
$2 + 2 + 0 = 4$. The sign of $x_1$ must be opposite to the rest here.

feedback.correct: Three of the five make row 1 vanish.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put each vector into $x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3$ and keep those giving 0.

byKey.c: You left out the zero vector. $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$, so it is in every nullspace.

explain.text: $(1, 1, -1) = \mathbf{s}_1 - \mathbf{s}_2$ and $(3, 0, -1) = -\mathbf{s}_2$, and $\mathbf{0}$ uses zero weights. The other two fail row 1. The nullspace is a plane through the origin in 3D.

screens.title: Every column a pivot
screens.prose: A new matrix, $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. One elimination step gives the pivots.
screens.question: What is $N(\mathbf{A})$?

options.why: A line needs a free variable. Both columns have pivots, so neither variable is free.
$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ always gives $\mathbf{0}$. The nullspace is never empty.

hints.text: Both columns have a circled pivot.
Row 2 gives $x_2 = 0$, and row 1 then gives $x_1 = 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve the reduced rows from the bottom up with right-hand side 0.

explain.text: Back substitution gives $x_2 = 0$, then $x_1 = 0$. With a pivot in every column, $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ forces $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$. This is what happens for every invertible matrix.

options.text: No. $\mathbf{A}$ is not the zero matrix, so only $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ works.
options.why: Non-zero entries do not stop cancelling. The columns $(1, -2)$ and $(-1, 2)$ point opposite ways, so one of each cancels.
Check it: $(1 + 1, -2 - 2) = (2, -4)$. The columns must cancel, so give them equal weights.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Eliminate first, then look for a column without a pivot.

byKey.nonzero-matrix: Non-zero entries do not stop cancelling. The columns $(1, -2)$ and $(-1, 2)$ point opposite ways, so one of each cancels.

explain.text: Elimination, $R_2 + 2R_1$, turns row 2 into zeros. Column 2 has no pivot, so $x_2$ is free, and $x_2 = 1$ gives $x_1 = 1$. $N(\mathbf{A})$ is the line through $(1, 1)$.

screens.prose: You followed the same steps each time. Eliminate. Each column without a pivot gives a free variable. Set one free variable to 1 and the rest to 0, then solve: a special solution. $$N(\mathbf{A}) = \{\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\} = \{c_1\mathbf{s}_1 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf{s}_k\}$$
screens.question: A $3 \times 5$ matrix has pivots in 3 of its columns. How many special solutions does $N(\mathbf{A})$ have?

options.why: That counts the pivot columns. Special solutions come from the columns without a pivot.
That counts every column. Only the free ones give special solutions.
Three equations cannot pin down five unknowns. Two stay free.

feedback.correct: $5 - 3 = 2$ free variables, one special solution each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the columns with no pivot.

explain.text: Five columns, three with pivots, leaves two free variables. Each gives one special solution. $N(\mathbf{A})$ is every combination of those two: a plane through the origin in 5D.

screens.prose: Here is the general solution of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ for $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\end{pmatrix}$, line by line.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 0$, the one equation left after elimination
$\mathbf{x} = (-2x_2 - 3x_3,\ x_2,\ x_3)$, write the whole input using the free variables
$\mathbf{x} = x_2(-2, 1, 0) + x_3(-3, 0, 1)$, split by free variable: $x_2\mathbf{s}_1 + x_3\mathbf{s}_2$

hints.text: Solve for the pivot variable before writing the vector.
The last line separates the $x_2$ terms from the $x_3$ terms.

feedback.correct: Eliminate, solve for the pivot variable, then split by free variable.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the equation left after elimination.

byKey.d3: You can only write $\mathbf{x}$ in free variables once $x_1$ is solved for.
byKey.d4: Splitting by free variable needs the whole vector written out first.

explain.text: Elimination leaves one equation, which fixes $x_1$. Writing $\mathbf{x}$ through $x_2$ and $x_3$ and splitting gives $x_2\mathbf{s}_1 + x_3\mathbf{s}_2$. The special solutions are exactly the vectors you found earlier.

screens.title: A trade that changes nothing
screens.prose: A portfolio holds stocks A, B and C. The table gives each stock’s exposure per £1 held. A trade $\mathbf{t}$, in £ bought, changes the exposures by $\mathbf{E}\mathbf{t}$. A trade in $N(\mathbf{E})$ changes neither exposure.
screens.question: You buy £10,000 of A. How much of C must you trade so that neither exposure changes? Enter a sale as a negative amount.

widget.label: Amount of C bought, in pounds
widget.accept: $-20000$: sell £20,000 of C, after buying £10,000 each of A and B.

hints.text: Size must stay unchanged too. What does that force you to do in B?

feedback.correct: Buy £10,000 of A and of B, sell £20,000 of C.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\mathbf{E}\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{0}$ as two equations, one per row, and solve.

byKey.sign: Buying more C would add beta. To cancel the beta you added, you sell C.
byKey.beta-only: You cancelled the beta of A alone. Size forces you to buy £10,000 of B as well, which adds beta too.
byKey.one-for-one: Swapping £1 for £1 ignores the betas and the size row. Solve both rows of $\mathbf{E}\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{0}$.

explain.text: The size row forces $b = a = 10000$. The beta row then needs $12000 + 8000 + c = 0$, so $c = -20000$. The trade also costs nothing net, $10000 + 10000 - 20000 = 0$: it reshuffles the book and leaves every exposure where it was.

ideas: The nullspace $N(\mathbf{A})$ holds every $\mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$. It always contains $\mathbf{0}$.
Eliminate. Each column without a pivot gives a free variable and one special solution.
$N(\mathbf{A})$ is every combination of the special solutions. It is a line, a plane, or just $\mathbf{0}$ when every column has a pivot.

formula.name: Nullspace
formula.note: Special solutions: one free variable 1, the others 0.

summary.trap: Non-zero entries do not mean only $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ works. Columns can cancel.

options.why: You dropped the minus sign: $3 + 3 = 6$, not 0.
You set the pivot variable to 1. The free variable $x_2$ is the one set to 1.
That is the first row of $\mathbf{A}$, not an input it sends to zero.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the free variable to 1 and solve for the other.

explain.text: Set $x_2 = 1$. Then $x_1 + 3 = 0$, so $x_1 = -3$. Every multiple of $(-3, 1)$ is in $N(\mathbf{A})$.

quiz.prose: After elimination, $\mathbf{U} = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&2\\0&1&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Column 3 has no pivot.
quiz.question: In the special solution, $x_3 = 1$. What is $x_1$?

byKey.row2: That is $x_2$, from row 2: $x_2 - 1 = 0$. Row 1 gives $x_1$.

explain.text: Row 1: $x_1 + 2(1) = 0$, so $x_1 = -2$. Row 2: $x_2 - 1 = 0$, so $x_2 = 1$. The special solution is $(-2, 1, 1)$.

options.why: $\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{s}) = \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{b}$, so $\mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{s}$ works too.
Any multiple $c\mathbf{s}$ is also in the nullspace, so every $\mathbf{x}_p + c\mathbf{s}$ works.

feedback.correct: Adding any nullspace vector leaves $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ unchanged.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x}_p + c\mathbf{s}) = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_p + c\mathbf{A}\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{0}$. So each $c$ gives a solution. A non-zero nullspace rules out a unique solution.

quiz.prose: Two stocks both have market beta 1.5. A trade buys £$a$ of the first and £$b$ of the second.
quiz.question: Which trades leave the portfolio beta unchanged?

options.why: $\mathbf{E} = (1.5,\ 1.5)$ has a free variable. Buying £1 of one and selling £1 of the other adds $1.5 - 1.5 = 0$.
Buying both adds $1.5a + 1.5a = 3a$ of beta. The two amounts must cancel.

explain.text: The beta change is $1.5a + 1.5b$. It is zero when $b = -a$: a line of trades, the nullspace of $\mathbf{E} = (1.5,\ 1.5)$. Switching between two stocks with the same beta changes no beta.
